The codebook adaptation feedback method using lookup tables, introduced approximately a decade ago for FDD configurations, has gained significant interest once more due to the FDD specifications being considered for 5G. Due to the increased data rates achievable with 20 MHz bandwidth, researchers have re-examined this method across seven different scenarios, assessing them at low, medium, and high mobility settings. This investigation utilized simulated downlink data to evaluate codebooks generated from Gaussian mixture models, in this case, representing the probability distributions of received signal constellations. In investigation, we compared these GMM-based lookup tables to traditional methods, and found that they performed well across both highly and loosely mobile settings in all examined scenarios.

A key aspect of quantum systems under periodic driving forces is their ability to maintain well-defined, stable nonequilibrium states that resist various types of disorder, and in multiple dimensions, these robust nonequilibrium states often exhibit rich topological characteristics. In recent experiments with cold atoms, a topologically characteristic surface state was discovered that persists despite perturbations in a two-dimensional Hofstadter lattice. Our theoretical investigation using the 3D Hofstadler model reveals multiple, distinct mechanisms generating such robust surface states and identifies the conditions under which these states display various topological properties. Our findings provide crucial guidance for experimentalists in their ongoing search for robust surface states in their three-dimensional setups.

When considering how massive objects behave under general relativity, the Bondi mass rate reduction rate has a minimum threshold. This research identifies the smallest possible value for that rate, denoted as $\left|\dot{M}_{\text{Bondi}}\right|$, by examining the field equations' constraints, taking into account their inherent relationship and mathematical properties. In a flat spacetime, we find that $\left|\dot{M}_{\text{Bondi}}\right| \ge 0$. However, in more complex scenarios, such as those around black holes, the rate is found to be at least 1/3 $\frac{8\pi G}{c^6}$ times the fifth power of the mass and the speed of sound squared, times the fourth power of the rate of change of a dimensionless parameter. This rate-limiting factor may have significant implications for understanding massive object behavior and the evolution of the gravitational wave spectrum.

The initial stars that formed in the Milky Way and other galaxies are believed to have been situated near the centers of their host galaxies, within dense concentrations known as nuclear star clusters. These star clusters are thought to have produced significant amounts of heavy elements, potentially contributing to the metal-rich environments observed in the galactic cores today. Our three-dimensional simulations reveal the remnant cores of these first stars were given substantial velocities through interactions with massive black holes in the clusters, resulting in the gravitational waves detected by LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA. Furthermore, our model predicts a specific pattern of early heavy element formation, characterized by the presence of stars with extremely high metallicities found in the centers of the galaxy.

In this work, we investigate and enhance the security of wireless transmissions using external antenna systems with four interconnected components: an arbitrary number of transmit and receive antennas and two external antennas for sending and receiving. The system uses wireless links with frequency subdivision and we focus on assessing and boosting its security performance. A primary transmit external antenna is used to relay information from encased transmit antennas via a relay in an attempt to conceal information from an eavesdropper who is listening in on the wireless transmission. The amount of security capacity of this system is characterized and the issue of maximizing this security capacity is investigated when different amounts of power can be used on each of the wireless transmission frequencies. When there is no interference from the eavesdropper, we determine the amount of effective data that can be transmitted securely and when there is eavesdropping we investigate different strategies to maximize this amount. Additionally, when there are many available frequencies to transmit on and we want to use the least amount of power possible, we determine the most effective way to distribute this power to ensure secure transmission. Finally, when some of the links between the system's components are not working properly we determine the most effective way to use available power to maximize security capacity and when there are limited amounts that can be used on each of the frequencies.

Our research introduced TextWorldExpress, a third version of the TextWorld simulator, which significantly enhances its processing speed to one million updates per second. By utilizing optimized data structures and techniques such as memory preallocation and vectorization, this third version of the TextWorld framework achieved a processing speed 10 times faster than the second version. When combined with the most efficient environment, it provided a 50 times faster update rate compared to the Python-based TextWorld framework. We also conducted a thorough analysis of the bottlenecks affecting simulation speed, offering actionable insights for developers aiming to create high-performance simulators.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on LSTM, have achieved significant success in various video analysis tasks. However, their large size poses challenges for deployment on resource-constrained devices for real-time video processing. To address this limitation, this study explores the potential of a hybrid architecture, combining lightweight mobile devices and a high-performance server. By utilizing a carefully designed hardware system and an optimized hierarchical LSTM network, the proposed method enables a more efficient and scalable video processing workflow. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the hardware system providing substantial speedup and energy savings compared to traditional server-based processing. Furthermore, the results are comparable to state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the balance between accuracy and efficiency achieved through this novel method.

If we consider a state in a conformal field theory that has no external gravitational effects and is made up of two subsets, A and B, we can examine two operators, X_A and X_B, whose correlations are protected from changing by any form of quantum entanglement in spacetime. These operators are said to be "lightly charged" in relation to this state. In the context of the holographic principle, where the conformal field theory is represented by anti-de Sitter space, we found that this "light-charge" property is maintained even in more complex states, as long as the corresponding geometric space remains within a certain "light-gravity" region relative to where the original state is located. This "light-charge" property is also observed in CFTs that describe flat or hyperbolic spaces. Furthermore, we developed a way to use this "light-charge" concept to prove the "heavy-light" inequality in double-trace CFTs, discovered the same property in specific models of CFTs in the description of flat space gravity, and even used it to reprove the "positivity of energy" principle within these models.

Given a local ring, we define the tight Hilbert polynomial as the one with the smallest coefficient magnitude, and denote the set of its roots as $\text{THar}(f)$. It is proven that $R$ is F-pure if and only if its element $x$ has empty $T$-number or an integer $c$ such that the quotient module $x^{q-1}$ and $\varphi_q(x^{q-1})$ are not zero for all integers $q \ge s$. Additionally, we characterize local rings by the property that the tight Hilbert polynomial has no non-zero integer aspects, relating this to the $F$-finite Gorenstein ring's $F$-purity. If the ring's quotient field has characteristic zero, it is shown that the ring is regular if and only if it is $F$-pure. We also establish an $F$-purity criterion based on the reduction of a scheme over a ring of characteristic zero to one over a finite $p$-adic ring.

This paper explores key considerations for designing effective supplementary services mechanisms to safeguard system reliability. The primary challenges addressed by these mechanisms are brief, informal summaries of the processes and structures underlying the main markets, which vary across main, option, and forward contracts, are examined in this research. The analysis is supported by a three-period game theory model that encompasses main, supplementary, and no-supplementary services markets. Through comparative studies, the model yields general insights into the buying patterns of utility in relation to the mechanisms established, thereby providing a framework for understanding market behavior. The resulting understanding can be directly applied to the development of targeted strategies for enhancing main markets and preventing supply shortfalls, along with recommendations for incorporating game theory models in the design of energy market mechanisms. The findings of this research are intended to support the broader community of researchers and professionals who study and work on the design of energy market mechanisms.

Let K be a field and $K\langle x\rangle$ be the ring of non-commutative polynomials in the variable x that is free over K. We are investigating how the factorization properties of a product of polynomials change under the iteration of a composition of functions. In particular, we are examining the way the factorization of a polynomial f^n(x^n) is related to the factorization of an integer n when expressed as the sum of two coprime squares.

High-altitude polar vortex formations in the atmospheres of outer planets, particularly at the boundary between mesosphere and stratosphere, have been extensively studied. In the past month, the infrared imaging capabilities of the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope allowed for the detection of a high-altitude, temperature-based polar vortex in the atmosphere of Saturn's north. By analyzing this polar vortex, researchers found that it was situated within a hexagonal cloud pattern with unusually high rotational and radial variations. Unlike previous observations, this hexagon shows a counterclockwise rotation, a feature that matches the expectations based on the gas dynamics theory of rotating systems. Furthermore, there is evidence of a recently discovered, small-scale P-vortex within the Saturnine hexagon's structure.

This study examines solutions to a Schr\"odinger equation with a convex obstacle. It is proven that non-linear equations with convex potential do not exhibit explosions. Additionally, for non-linear equations without energy loss, we provide conditions under which explosions do not occur.

Let $K$ represent a field with a characteristic of positive value and let $A$ be a finitely generated subfield of the rational numbers within $K$. This study aims to create efficient methods for creating locally optimized solutions to finding the most efficient expressions of the coordinates of a geometric shape - an affine variety defined by prime ideals in a polynomial ring over $K$ with unknowns $x_1, \dots, x_n$ - using the $A$-coefficients in its shape's description. This is particularly relevant in the study of geometric shapes over fields with a characteristic of positive value.

The concept of simplicial collections was first introduced by Lurie in his work on higher chromatic homotopy theory, and it was proved that the simplicial category of graded collections has the same morphism structure as the derived category of linearly grown graded modules. Building on this proof, we establish two key properties: the polarization of the simplicial category of linearly grown collections and the equivalence of the simplicial category of rational graded collections to its graded counterpart, which then allows for the extension of the localization theorem from classical derived categories to its graded version.

This work examines fundamental measures from the theory of orbital integrals, originating from Iwasima in 1949, and explores significant extensions, most notably the Tamagawa number, initially introduced by Tamagawa in 1960. Our investigation offers concise yet comprehensive proofs for key theorems from both the Iwasima and Tamagawa frameworks, providing concise demonstrations for fundamental results concerning orbital measures, as well as more sophisticated ones, including the Gauss manifestation, the Siegel heuristic, and the Tate heuristic. Furthermore, our analysis also delivers proofs for additional measures, including those introduced by Poitou in 1956 and Kurokawa in 2005, as well as an examination of Tamagawa numbers for specific varieties, including those of Weil in 1948.

Using a Foxboro type steam generator model, we developed a method to calculate in real-time the liquid level inside the drum through the analysis of a neutron diffusion spectrum. A key aspect of this approach involves a mathematical expression that determines how x-ray signals shift based on the Neutron Energy Equation. After a test with a 110 kVp x-ray source and a thick copper filter, our approach enabled accurate determination of the neutron diffusion spectrum and subsequently the level of liquid within the drum, as demonstrated in this study.

We present a new mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured media. Our approach offers the flexibility to work with general polygonal meshes and accurately models both high-permeability fractures and a low-permeability matrix. We develop a local projection-based method to incorporate the source and interface terms into our discrete formulation, resulting in an equivalent system of equations. To solve this system, we apply a series of transformations to eliminate certain variables and obtain a simplified equation involving only pressure. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that our technique produces reliable results with optimal convergence rates for pressure and velocity, as well as excellent capacity to capture interface peaks on highly conductive fractures.

The Bayes factor stands out as a dependable method for hypothesis testing, effectively overcoming many issues that plague other approaches. However, its application requires thorough computation of the Bayes' theorem's numerator, which can be time-consuming for complex models and leave researchers' alternative models in question for extended periods. To address this challenge, we introduce a suite of R packages designed to automate the calculation of the Bayes factor through model comparison, enabling seamless integration into statistical modeling workflows. These tools allow for effortless model competition among multiple models by calculating the background model's evidence, facilitating visual exploration and debugging through evidence-based plotting and debugging features. Moreover, the suite enables the incorporation of Bayes factors into mixed-effects models through model sampling, thereby enhancing the scientific rigor of Bayesian analysis. By leveraging the automated Bayes factor computation, the bar for rejecting an alternative model in Bayesian studies is raised, promoting the development of more credible alternative models and increasing the value of Bayesian methods.

Discourse indicators such as "you know", "well", and "so" are commonly used in human communication to convey additional meaning within a conversation. However, this can lead to fillers that obstruct effective communication and, as a result, computer systems that depend on written communication struggle to process signals buried within the noise. This research investigates the semantic content of indicators voluntarily used in conversations with a chatbot, distinguishing between those that add value to the conversation and those that are merely noise. A new annotated dataset called Discourse Semantics is created to classify the meaning of indicators, which is then used to train and test various models to examine the semantics of discourse signals. A comparison is made between different approaches, revealing that a category-based system successfully captures the meaning of indicators used voluntarily in conversations with a chatbot.

When training deep neural networks, large matrices are a common parameter space that we navigate, and a variety of optimization methods, including least squares and gradient descent, are employed to solve the resulting matrix optimization problems. A fundamental challenge in this field is to understand the impact of non-convexity on these problems. This paper aims to address this challenge by applying the concept of geodesic convexity, a more lenient non-convex property, to the non-convex low-rank matrix optimization problem. We find a problem landscape devoid of spurious minima and saddle points, with only convex regions remaining. As a result, any starting point and step size in this problem space guarantees a solution that continuously decreases or maximizes the expected loss function. These findings hold significant implications for the design of neural network architectures and provide a unique perspective on parameter spaces that were previously unexamined. In particular, this work introduces a novel approach to neural network training, where we treat the parameter space as a curved surface rather than a flat one. By using this new perspective, we develop a geodesically convex training algorithm for a popular class of neural networks, with global convergence guarantees. This algorithm combines standard methods with a range of step sizes to minimize the loss function, with linear complexity costs.

A graph is considered edge-tintable with cubic parts if its edges can be colored either white or red such that each vertex is connected by at least one red edge. This paper begins by exploring the relationship between 2-factorizations and edge-tinting in cubic bipartite graphs, initially confining our examination to these graphs. Ultimately, however, our edge-tinting examination of cubic graphs extends beyond the cubic bipartite limitations.

In a computer simulation of symmetric Cournot games, a population of agents with genetically encoded evolutionary strategies competed and reached equilibrium through natural selection. We tested two evolutionary algorithms, steady-state genetics and rotating pools, using a simple encoding scheme that facilitated efficient population-wide learning. Agents participated in a round-robin tournament, dynamically adjusting their production levels based on the total output of the population. Over time, the population evolved to maximize its average winnings, approaching the optimal equilibrium of the game. Notably, this was achieved without any agent knowing about the underlying game's rules. However, when the underlying game's parameters changed, the population struggled to adapt. We also compared our results to a more complex genetic encoding known to overfit the strategies required to reach the optimal equilibrium. Our research contributes to the understanding of evolutionary strategies for establishing equilibrium in economic interactions and learning algorithms for solving matrix-free, high-dimensional problems.

Consider a weighted directed graph G, and let I_G represent its edge ideal. Our study categorizes G's (or a subgraph's) structure based on the relationship between its ordinary and symbolic ideals, and specifically characterizes (acyclic) quasisymmetric graphs in terms of its structure.

Artificial Intelligence systems, particularly those based on Machine Learning, are essential for safety-critical applications like self-driving cars and medical imaging analysis. Nevertheless, their reliability in ensuring safety and preventing accidents is a pressing concern. Neural Network algorithms, which are pivotal to the performance of these AI systems, are vulnerable to various types of cyberattacks and physical faults that can cause undetected alterations in their behavior. Such alterations can result in catastrophic failures, endangering human lives. While proposals for secure AI implementations using cryptography and fault-tolerant computing exist, a significant amount of work on these approaches is experimental in nature and lacks theoretical underpinnings. In contrast, this work presents a framework for evaluating the security of TITAN, a neural network system that integrates advanced hardware for real-time anomaly detection with robust data preprocessing. Furthermore, it proposes interval-based verification as an alternative to adversarial examples for ensuring trustworthy AI implementations, exemplified through analyses of the safety mechanisms in TITAN and the Gradient Boosting Classifier.

The Jordanian twist, commonly used in the context of Toda field theories, undergoes a family of deformations that are examined, specifically one-parameter in nature. A specific deformation value is identified that is idempotent, resulting in a modified twist deformation with reduced strength. Another scenario with distinct behavior is identified at an infinitely high deformation value, in particular, this is associated with the Toda field theory with $SU(3)$ algebra, which exhibits different coupling strengths for various interactions within the theory. Despite these differences, the deformation's effect remains consistent, leading to a doubly periodic family with characteristics that are mapped out.

Cross-lingual semantic alignment is a challenging task, especially for low-resource languages. A key hurdle is constructing a unified semantic space that captures the intricate cluster structures of each language's vocabulary, which, as we've observed, often don't align well across languages. Our approach, called Cluster-consistent Word Representation (CWR), builds on a proven method, aligning both global and local information, including word-level similarities and cluster-level relationships, across multiple languages. CWR uses a flexible, modular design, allowing it to effectively transfer knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages. In experiments, CWR outperformed previous methods in code-switched machine translation and simultaneous translation tasks, demonstrating its ability to create a more robust, multi-lingual semantic space, even when working with languages that have vastly different resource levels.

Measurements have been made of the production of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons across various transverse momentum ranges in Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. Ratios of produced particles have been analyzed in relation to net-charges within accepted rapidity ranges. When viewed in relation to those of Au-Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 7.7$ TeV and Cu-Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 3.9$ TeV, the production of $\phi$ mesons in high-momentum ranges in Xe-Xe collisions appears suppressed. The transverse momentum distributions of Xe-Xe produced particles have been fitted using a Bose-Einstein probability function to obtain estimates of average particle momentum, which are in line with theoretical predictions based on thermal models. The Xe-Xe collisions exhibit a similar radii estimate to that of Au-Au and Cu-Cu collisions at the same rapidity, indicating a comparable initial state temperature and radii.

In the fall of 2019, Chile experienced widespread unrest driven by public discontent over socioeconomic issues and a particularly unpopular train robbery. This disorder escalated from isolated incidents to extensive demonstrations and riots that shook the country, culminating in the overthrow of the government. This project aimed to analyze the spread of these protests over a one-month span in 2019 by applying an SIR epidemiological model adapted for its context. By treating the demonstrations like an infectious disease and utilizing actual data to estimate unknown variables, researchers fitted the model to monthly statistics from seven distinct regions. Furthermore, they explored various scenarios to determine how different factors influenced the trajectory of the protests.

This research focuses on establishing a decision method for inequalities involving stars, plus signs, question marks, and concatenation in extended regular expressions over a quasi-order relation defined on regular expressions with alphabets $\Sigma$. To achieve this, we first define the preorder generated by these expressions based on their underlying languages, and then examine whether one expression is greater than or equal to another according to this preorder. Furthermore, we develop a closure operation that allows us to convert the original alphabet $\Sigma$ into an expanded alphabet $\Sigma'$ while preserving the precedence order relation, and ultimately propose the use of automaton-based techniques to verify inequalities involving these expressions.

Mobile agents often struggle to accurately locate important objects in their environment due to excessive drift in their position estimation over time. Our new technique, EMA Visual Navigation, develops a compact, external memory to efficiently estimate depth and objects' positions. By utilizing a specially designed memory access method, our model pays closer attention to the objects' locations, resulting in a significant reduction in positioning errors, as evidenced in our study's findings. Our experiments showed our approach's position estimation accuracy improved by 28.1%, 44.1%, and 55.6% across different scenarios when compared to the current leading technique. Our code is freely available online at https://github.com/hhhuang/External-Memory-Focus-VI-Navigation.

A new type of Weyl semimetal, which we've dubbed "sorted-Weyl", is introduced in this paper, with its sorted bulk band structure consisting of ERSE and SEORE components near the Fermi energy. This sorted structure is a byproduct of strong spin-orbit coupling in certain elevated-order topological insulators and can be maintained under conditions where the elevated-order topology is preserved. Our research reveals that sorted-Weyl and conventional elevated-order Weyl semimetals both possess robust surface and edge/arc states with unique characteristics and coupling mechanisms. By doping an sorted-Weyl TI with electron donors, we developed a sorted-Quantum Anomalous Hall effect and helical edge states on the same interface, and our findings are relevant for both fundamental and practical applications.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a data completion problem for Maxwell's equations. We propose a new formulation of this problem by framing it as the minimization of a cost function that combines the discrepancy between given and computed data with $L^2$-norm regularization terms for both the electric and magnetic fields. To effectively resolve this problem, we construct a numerical approach combining a boundary integral formulation for the unknown portion with a quasi-reversibility method for determining the unknown boundary. The accuracy of our method is demonstrated through several numerical experiments.

For knowledge systems to remain effective, they need to adapt by absorbing new information from various sources. When different systems contribute their data through a process called knowledge fusion, ensuring the absorbed information matches the original system's style is a significant challenge. A recent paper explores the difficulty of integrating decentralized, extra knowledge that is only partially visible and not fully accessible. In this process, a server collects data from multiple clients in a decentralized manner. It's a significant challenge because the knowledge from each client may not be compatible with the server's existing structure. As a result, simply combining the knowledge can be detrimental. To address this challenge, the server can choose to integrate knowledge from certain clients while rejecting the rest, a process known as federated selective integration. This paper examines a specific scenario where clients' knowledge systems are of equal size to the server's. Using game theory, it discovered that the optimal strategy is to divide the rejection rate in a way that maximizes the performance of the system. Furthermore, numerical results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness and its ability to achieve the desired outcomes.

For any finite group G, we define the Riemann hypothesis constant $\gamma_G$ as the greatest common divisor of |G| and the orders of its proper subgroups. We investigate the relationship between $\gamma_G$ and the extent of splitting of the rational number field for itquatic extensions defined by polynomials with coefficients that make them irreducible over the integers and whose associated Galois group is a subgroup of G for some symmetric group $S_n$. In particular, we find that for the alternating group $A_4$, $\gamma_{A_4}$ equals 12, indicating that these polynomials force the splitting of the rational number field up to an $A_4$ quartic extension. Similarly, for the symmetric group $S_4$, we determine that $\gamma_{S_4}$ equals 8, indicating that these polynomials force the splitting of the rational number field up to an $S_4$ quartic extension at most. These findings are illustrated through explicit examples for both $A_4$ and $S_4$ and involve determining the minimal degree of extension of the rational numbers unramified at infinity in which $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{-1}$ can be expressed.

We investigate the rate at which entanglement grows in a broad class of quantum field theories with holographic duals under a wide range of initial conditions and in various spatial dimensions. By utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence, we establish an upper bound on this entanglement growth rate that is analogous to the Quantum Null Energy Condition (QNEC). Unlike its quantum field theory-derived counterpart, our holographic-based upper bound has a distinct, geometric meaning. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which entanglement growth rate can become unbounded, both geometrically and within the context of quantum field theory. Additionally, we calculate the entanglement growth rate for anti-de Sitter space and compare it to the bounds we derived, finding that neither the QNEC nor its holographic equivalent is saturated in this case. We also explore the implications of our findings for the entropy of shock waves in both gravitating and non-gravitating theories.

Determining the minimum time required for a quantum system to evolve from an arbitrary initial state to a orthogonal state under time-varying Hamiltonians is a key aspect of quantum dynamics research.  A 2014 study by Brunner et al. demonstrated that for a single qubit, this time could be directly related to a simpler measure known as the quantum asymmetry. Due to its visual representation in the Bloch ball, researchers found this method intuitive and easy to apply. Since then, multiple groups have expanded this research to encompass more complex quantum systems. In this study, we derive a mathematical formula that links the fiducial time to changes in quantum asymmetry, providing a fresh perspective on speed limits in single-qubit systems. Notably, we also highlight the limitations of using quantum asymmetry as a guide for estimating speed limits in single-qubit systems. As an alternative, we introduce two new asymmetry metrics that can be directly used to minimize speed limits for single-qubit systems. Furthermore, we show that for unitary evolutions of a single qubit under a fixed Hamiltonian, the quantum majorization order of the initial and target states' quantum asymmetries must be satisfied. This condition allows us to establish more restrictive lower bounds on the admissible time required for such unitary transformations to take place.

Consider a unit interval, denoted as $I = [0, 1]$, and let's take the Cartesian product of this interval with itself, resulting in $I^2$. Let $\mathcal{P}_n$ represent the collection of polynomials with a maximum degree of $n$. We're interested in the norm of a specific interpolation operator, $L$, that maps the collection of continuous functions on $I^2$, denoted as $C(I^2)$, to the collection of polynomials with a degree of $n$, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_n$. This operator $L$ is defined by an interpolation process on a lattice $\xi$. The norm of this interpolation operator, when calculated with respect to the supremum norm, is denoted as $\|L\|$. It has been established that $\|\|L\|\geq 1$ for any lattice $\xi$ and a wide range of values for $n$. However, it has also been shown that $\|\|L\|\leq (2n+1)^2$ for certain lattices and $\|\|L\|\leq 2.11^n$ for other lattices.

Microwave technology under 10 GHz is highly established, but it faces increasing competition from terahertz frequencies, which offer greater bandwidth for applications like 5G/6G and are known to cause electromagnetic radiation concerns. However, a key advantage of microwave frequencies is the ability to miniaturize components, which is critical for certain devices. To determine if this miniaturization is achievable in the terahertz frequency range, researchers have recently created sub-10 GHz microwave circuits at extremely small scales, such as 1mm, while using near-field terahertz nanoscopy for detailed analysis. This technique revealed that radio-frequency components can indeed operate successfully in the terahertz frequency range with little interference, confirming their compatibility and providing a foundation for the coexistence of microwave and terahertz frequencies, which is essential for certain applications like quantum computing that combine both frequency ranges.

This article examines the complex and ongoing atmospheric development of Venus by drawing on recent research and observations from various sources, including the successful VEGA landings, data from the Venus Express, and images from the Solar and Wind Terrestrial Explorer. We analyze the role of different components within the atmosphere, on the surface, and in the clouds, and their interplay in a range of timescales. We also consider alternative theories to the standard development model, including the potential impact of large meteorites, the effects of the planet's slow rotation, and the influence of surface heat on the atmosphere's circulation patterns. Ultimately, we consider how recent data can be used to refine simulations and models to better understand the continuous and cyclical nature of the atmosphere's development on Venus.

We have developed a Bayesian inference method for a Hawkes process with a quadratic decay function in memory, aimed at capturing realistic memory effects in point process data. By incorporating a non-linear link function and a general kernel function, this model can effectively model both short and long memory characteristics observed in real-world datasets. Utilizing a Gaussian random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, Bayesian inference for the non-linear Hawkes model has been achieved with the suitability of the sampler verified through an exact simulation method. A Bayesian approach to hypothesis testing for the memory characteristic of a point process has also been demonstrated using the Hawkes process model. A case study involving intraday depth data from New York Stock Exchange has further showcased the advantages of the non-linear Hawkes model in comparison to traditional linear versions over multiple datasets.

Concurrent amplification and modification of laser pulse polarizations are highly relevant concepts to investigate in the context of advanced plasma physics. When a circularly polarized, high-intensity and ultra-short laser beam interacts with a plasma containing a transverse magnetic field, linearly polarized components emerge and become significant at frequencies near the plasma frequency. This study explores the mechanisms governing the modification and enhancement of these plasma frequencies. It is found that for sub-relativistic regimes, electron nonlinearity results in a shift of frequency while plasma deflection leads to a broadening of the signal. As intensity increases to the relativity realm, electron nonlinearity causes a blue shift in frequency, with a distinct behavior observed at the 5/3/2 critical intensity threshold. It is notable that for a specific range of plasma frequencies, the polarization shifts from linear to elliptical before reverting to linear. As the intensity of the laser pulses is reduced and the pulses lengthen, mixtures of different frequencies emerge. This research provides a robust theoretical foundation for a novel diagnostic tool to investigate plasma properties using high-intensity and ultrashort laser pulses.

Re-evaluulating the upper limit of the tau lepton's electric dipole strength, our analysis considers deep-inelastic scattering and hadron production processes involving tau hadrons. By applying these processes and a comprehensive theoretical framework based on parton distribution functions and the operator product expansion, our findings are evaluated. In particular, we find that the tau lepton's electric dipole moment constraint within this framework is marginally higher than the current limit, predicting a value of |d_τ| < 5.0 × 10^(-17) e·cm, within the operator product expansion approach.

We provide a decoding algorithm for rank metric codes that achieves a decision radius of $\sigma/2$, where $\sigma$ indicates the code's symmetry. If the code is not inherently symmetric, we also present a -1 log q erasure-free decoding algorithm with the ability to resolve up to $\sigma/2$ errors of rank $r$. The proposed decoding scheme can be applied to Mitran-Shamir-Tse's rank metric TAC code, offering a decision radius of $/2$ and resolving its previously unaddressed downside.

In the context of a conformal field theory with global symmetry, we investigate the structure of operator product expansions, specifically focusing on four primary operators that form a global representation. Notably, we examine conditions under which higher-spin currents can appear in these representations. A key constraint we consider is whether such currents can have non-zero three-point correlations with external fields. When three-point correlations are forbidden, we demonstrate how the dynamics can be understood through the exchange of specific intermediate states, including an anti-free field, during correlation calculations of four external operators. Furthermore, we show how this approach can be adapted to conformal field theory in anti-de Sitter space, involving bosonic and fermionic fields of various spins, interacting through the exchange of specific intermediate states, including an anti-free field in three-dimensional space.

This research paper focuses on Gelfand and MacPherson's groundbreaking categorical approach to establishing an algebraic formula for Pontrjagin classes. We first examine the key components of their groundbreaking transfer transformation method between functors, as applied to specific algebraic varieties. Subsequently, we analyze the underlying principles and specific steps involved in computing the $2n$-th Pontrjagin class using Gelfand-MacPherson's framework, comparing its results with established computations found in existing literature.

We are analyzing the data from SuperNova Factory for Lick Observatory (Supernova FOrescaster for Lick - SFOL) for the SN 2020jfo, which is a Type II supernova located in the NGC 253 galaxy. A short plateau phase of approximately 90 days was observed in its light curve along with a high H-alpha line equivalent width of 4.0 x 10^17 Angstroms, indicating a dense circumstellar medium. The host galaxy's inclination angle is 50.9 degrees with an H-alpha/Pa-alpha ratio of 0.90 that suggests a level of 4.1x10^23 cm^-2 in ionized gas within the stellar remnant. A relatively low H I column density of 5.4x10^21 cm^-2 was found in the SN 2020jfo host region. The SN 2020jfo spectrum on 86 days post-explosion allowed us to determine a projected speed of 955 km/s for the ionized hydrogen and an absolute magnitude of -16.52 for V band. The SFOL package was utilized to calculate the SN 2020jfo distance of 11.3 Mpc that aligns with values from previous studies.

Lenses with unusual structures have been extensively researched to enhance the natural reflecting properties of parabolic surfaces, enabling them to efficiently allow visible light to pass through while bending X-rays. At the surface, these innovative structures consist of a vast number of flexible shells resembling those of American lobsters, thus earning the name "lobster-eye lenses." These lenses have shown remarkable success in allowing wide-angle visible light vision for X-ray imaging applications, and are now being considered for use in a satellite designed to allow images of the X-ray sky to be produced in wide-ranging detail. However, to achieve high-resolution images in wide-field imaging, a significant number of individual lens elements must be tightly packed together, thus giving rise to new challenges in designing detector systems that can be used in conjunction with such lenses. In this study, we successfully applied lobster-eye lenses to a focal-plane detector system in order to produce wide-field mock-up images of the X-ray sky, and we also explored the possibility of using multiple cameras with lenses to build a novel concept for an all-encompassing B-field X-ray monitor.

We examine a specific approach to representing local ellipticity in partial differential equations, specifically a partial uniform ellipticity scheme. This method utilizes a "cutting" operation on a matrix that separates a portion of its spectrum, with the remaining part exhibiting uniform ellipticity. Our cutting PDE framework yields new proofs for several results, providing new proofs for the well-posedness and regularity in the oblique derivative problem with partially elliptic coefficients, as well as for the existence of solutions to the stochastic flag equation with non-Lipschitzian coefficients.

To accelerate large-scale simulations and reduce halo finding complexities, a new findings method based on linear velocity fields is widely used for initial simulations. Although the function is linear for small scales, the role of non-linear effects and how they need to be accounted for in halo finding simulations is unclear. This study employs the CRNLM and ANNR as tools to analyze the Dark Matter Halo Mass-Function relationship in the Lambda-CDM model, particularly beyond linear regimes. It is found that both ANNR and ANNR combine with linear halo finding models accurately reproduce the Mass-Function relationship, but a 20% discrepancy exists for lower mass halos when incorporating non-linear effects and that this error is too high for some applications. Notably, a ANNR model that is trained on linear data successfully replicates the Mass-Function relationship of simulated halos beyond $10^8 h^{-1} M_{\sun}$, a 0.1 accuracy level is reached for all halos. This study suggests a potential strategy to correct simulated halo distributions and paves the way for using halo finding models on large-scale simulations with significantly reduced computational costs.

We have developed a method to create balanced equations for rotating stars in
special relativity. This approach uses a set of variables that directly correspond
to a stationary and axisymmetric energy-momentum tensor, enabling us to formulate
these equations in terms of these variables. By and large, these equations can be
broken down into simpler components. This simplification includes separating the
transverse pressure into two parts: one part is perpendicular to the rotation's
axis, and the other is parallel to it. This allows us to focus on the equations
for stars rotating at speeds close to their maximum possible speed by applying a
specific approximation and simplifying the model further.

Existing document extraction models, such as CRIs, improve efficiency by automatically structuring visual documents, but they also increase dependency on externally labeled data. This progression makes reducing the requirement for extensive external annotation a pressing challenge. This challenge can be mitigated by using a novel framework called Visual Document Automatic Annotation (ViDAA), which generates annotations internally without access to externally labeled information. The ViDAA framework employs a set of tools to automatically generate annotations, including: (1) a method to represent sorted content in documents as sequence tags, (2) an approach to highlight visually distinct regions as shape tags, and (5) a technique to mark table structures as shape tags. These annotations are then combined to generate comprehensive data labels. Furthermore, ViDAA can: (3) highlight areas of visual significance that require external expert annotation, and (4) utilize a carefully selected subset of visually complex documents for training exceptional extraction models while significantly cutting annotation expenses. Experiments conducted on four publicly accessible datasets, comprising both simple and complex structures, demonstrate the exceptional effectiveness of the ViDAA framework in enhancing the performance of extraction models, simultaneously producing high-quality data labels that are visually annotated. The results show a 0.86 average performance gain over randomly selected labels and a 96% reduction in the need for external data labeling. Additionally, the ViDAA framework achieves a 2.25 average performance boost over models trained on randomly selected documents while producing a set of visually annotated documents

With the advent of gravitational wave astronomy, a comprehensive understanding of neutron star mergers and black hole binaries is now within reach. To fully grasp NStoGW signals, particularly those involving NS-NS, NS-BH, and BH-BH combinations, a method to efficiently classify these events based on LIGO/Virgo observed data is crucial. A study is presented that leverages a novel generative model to create a vast and diverse dataset, enabling a deep learning classifier to accurately rank LIGO/Virgo waveforms along a one-dimensional continuum. This ranking system facilitates a compact and accurate classification of NS-NS, NS-BH, and BH-BH events directly from the injected waveform parameters, obviating the need for computationally intensive full-relativistic simulations. The model's efficiency is further highlighted by its ability to accurately classify a diverse dataset, even with varying levels of noise. To test the robustness of the classifier, the 17 NS-BH merger events detected by LIGO/Virgo since 2019 were re-analyzed, with the model's predictions closely aligning with original classifications in 16 out of 17 cases. The proposed method's potential to accelerate future analyses of NS mergers and enable timely multi-messenger astronomy is particularly promising.

Urban interactions are critical to the spread of infectious diseases and have a significant impact on economic development. During the COVID-19 pandemic, people's mobility patterns changed drastically in urban areas, leading to both short-term public health consequences and long-term economic disparities. In the context of Shanghai, our mobile device data analysis reveals that the pandemic resulted in considerable variation in mobility restrictions across different income levels, with a 10th percentile increase in over-constrained locations associated with a 19.3% drop in GDP growth. Our study also found that higher over-constraint in low-income areas was linked to lower future GDP growth, whereas there was no such effect observed in high-income areas. Our research also found that the pandemic-related disparities in urban interactions were substantially reduced following the relaxation of mobility controls, with no lasting impacts observed.

Numerous observations and theoretical findings suggest that the young massive stars in various cosmic regions form through a process involving the accumulation of discrete, high-mass events. To investigate the characteristics and nature of these events, we analyzed the early development phase of a particularly massive protostar, Asnomus A, within the Asnomus nebula. By examining a detailed model of this protostar that closely matches observational data, we discovered that the surrounding cloud near the protostar contained a number of dense, spherical events of varying sizes and locations. There was also significant evidence of dense event debris merging together in a network of streams and the formation of a massive event remnant near the star. Notably, simulations have demonstrated that both gravitational wave emission and event remnant merging can occur among these events. Furthermore, there was significant evidence of intense radiation being reflected and scattered by the events, suggesting that similar phenomena could be observable in other early stages of very massive star formation. As another crucial finding, the model revealed a process in which events could transfer enough momentum to the surrounding environment to significantly slow down the collapse of the cosmic cloud and allow for the formation of additional protoplanetary events of lower mass near the more massive one, as observed in some very massive star systems. In essence, viewing dense events as a key component in the formation process of very massive stars is a compelling and plausible event.

We derive an exact, non-trivial Hamiltonian version of the Dysthe equation as a water depth asymptotic limit for a system with uniform positive vorticity beneath the surface water. Our work builds on previous research that used canonical transformations to derive water depth limit systems, extending beyond canonical transformations to derive non-canonical asymptotic limits. We then establish the non-trivial water depth limit accuracy of the Dysthe equation for this system, showing the Hamiltonian form has a sequence of solutions with the same wavelength and amplitude over time, slowly varying according to the initial conditions within the set. This research can be seen as an extension of previous canonical asymptotic limit and time-average energy conservation studies. Ultimately, this allows us to derive a lower and upper bound on the time-average kinetic plus potential energy, showing the Dysthe equation underestimates the energy with a 10% to 20% margin for depths greater than 200 wavelengths.

This research extends the concepts of vector fields, one-forms, and the Stokes theorem to complex functions, also known as locally convex functions, providing expressions for these concepts in the context of such functions. These expressions contain the classical results as a subset of more comprehensive expressions. Furthermore, the paper proves that the set of all complex functions is not a vector space, demonstrating that the concepts of vector fields and one-forms must be defined as operations outside the framework of a vector space. Additionally, an expression for the divergence operator in the case of complex functions is derived both without and with homogeneous coordinates, while also presenting a geometric proof of this result. Finally, the paper applies these concepts to derive an expression for the balance of a quantity within a terrain with arbitrary boundary geometry through the use of an integral operator associated with a one-form defined by a vector field and a locally convex terrain.

The navigation systems of autonomous vehicles can become overwhelmed by the vast amount of dynamic objects in their surroundings, requiring real-time processing and blending of layers to effectively manage multiple layers simultaneously. In this paper, we introduce a layered navigation approach that incorporates real-time sensor data blending without delaying any individual object's path planning. Our proposed immediate sonar blending technique, applied to our four-layer navigation controller, achieves smoother movement and efficient obstacle avoidance by producing notable improvements over the original system's performance metrics. Experimental results show that the modified system significantly enhances smoothness and clearance while maintaining comparable obstacle avoidance capabilities.

The proliferation of digital media and the internet has significantly altered the way we consume information, but it has also given rise to a growing problem of online fraud, with deceptive news articles posing a serious threat to public safety and societal stability. With the explosive increase in the number of news articles being published, it has become nearly impossible for human moderators to manually monitor and detect fraudulent content at scale. To address this challenge, our study proposes a innovative framework that combines enhanced sequence-to-sequence models with a fraudulent news classification system based on the unique content of news articles. Our proposed framework achieves remarkable results, outperforming the best existing techniques in a range of evaluation metrics, including micro-F1, accuracy, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.

This study investigates the bending properties of $d$-dimensional i.i.d. Gaussian random fields defined over a discrete torus, focusing on the residual process after fitting a bent plane. The research establishes precise asymptotic behavior for the maximum and the second largest values of this residual process, demonstrating a form of stochastic strong approximation with an improved convergence rate of $n^{-1/2+\varepsilon}$. The findings extend previous findings from random processes to random fields and provide a bent version of the extremal process, thereby offering a justified bending principle in the context of random fields. Additionally, the proof techniques developed in this result have practical applications in spatial data analysis and gravitational wave detection.

When examining high-dimensional data with symmetry under rotations, a type of privacy infringement known as rotational invariance $\ell_1$-norm PCA aims to identify significant features or simplify its structure. A challenging aspect of this problem is that it lacks a convex property, which hinders the use of standard optimization methods typically employed in PCA. A new iterative algorithm is proposed in this work to address this problem, leveraging the underlying diversity of this scenario. This method converges to a correct solution at a linear rate under specific conditions, which are shown to be met in many practical applications. Moreover, theoretical and experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's efficiency and suitability for large-scale data sets.

Recent advances in natural language processing rely on semantic annotations, but these annotations are becoming outdated and inconsistent. This study focuses on updating and ensuring the quality of semantic annotations in the form of classification models based on new text inputs. Specifically, we examine a classification model for a unique dataset containing 1,100 texts with associated emotions from the 2020 Brazilian Presidential Election. This dataset includes a highly regarded baseline model from its creators that we replicate using the BERT architecture. Our work involves two main parts: first, we rebalance a dataset with skewed class distribution and compare the performance of resulting models; and second, we evaluate a combined dataset with equal proportions and a model derived from it. This study contributes a replicated baseline as well as new findings in the form of discussion points and comparison tables related to addressing imbalance in semantic annotations.

A significant challenge in autonomous vehicle navigation within unfamiliar environments is Navigating through Unknown Spaces. Successfully navigating uncharted territories is essential for space exploration and the operation of autonomous robots on other planets. Current map-based navigation systems struggle with limited generalizability due to their heavy reliance on predefined datasets. A key factor hindering the widespread use of these systems is their limited ability to adapt to new environments. In contrast, learning representations that facilitate successful navigation in untested uncharted spaces requires focus. This work proposes a novel cognitive map structure called a Hierarchical Topological Layout, comprising global, regional, and local components. This structure enables efficient, flexible navigation in previously untested spaces. We investigate a two-stage training approach comprising a prior Stage where vehicles learn to build a graphical map from sensor data, and a Stage where they are trained to navigate using this representation. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed system through performance evaluations in untested uncharted spaces.

Researchers utilized atomic interferometry to precisely detect minute local magnetic field variations caused by the superconducting Meissner effect's quantum phenomenon. This precise measurement technique allowed for a sensitive experiment on the quantum nature of the Meissner effect's effect on magnetic fields. Atomic interferometry enabled the comparison of measurements from both sides of a transition between the He II and He I helium phases to the extent of 10^-15 Tesla over 10 centimeters. This degree of precision is 10^6 times more precise than previous measurements, setting a precise standard for those measurements.

This study establishes a bridge between probability theory and probabilistic geometry, specifically showing that certain results from the gyration theory of distributions apply to mixture models. By demonstrating an connection, findings previously derived through statistical inference can now be reinterpreted and validated using a geometric approach, and conversely, the theorems of probabilistic geometry can now be validated within the context of mixture models. A crucial insight gained is that distributions with maximal flexibility in mixture models possess extended support, thus enabling the geometric techniques to be applied even with limited data sets. Moreover, a geometric derivation of the structure of Koopman distributions is obtained, and an investigation into their applicability in modeling is undertaken.

High-performance applications relying on machine learning models and neural networks often experience performance bottlenecks due to inefficient memory management on GPUs, particularly with their fragmented memory systems. These systems, characterized by a variety of memory objects with different lifespans and memory access patterns, exacerbate this issue. Existing GPU memory allocators fall short in addressing this challenge, as they are limited to concurrent garbage collection techniques or highly optimized, but not concurrent, memory reclamation methods. To overcome these limitations, a new class of GPU memory allocators is needed that combines excellent concurrent memory management capabilities. Inspired by cutting-edge research in concurrent data structures, our proposed object-oriented GPU memory allocator, DynaSOAr, integrates a handle-based reclamation technique with a specialized generation-based concurrent garbage collection method, GB-MarkAndScan, to effectively manage memory. DynaSOAr demonstrates superior memory efficiency compared to leading GPU memory allocators, reducing peak memory usage by up to 2.6 times and improving application performance by up to 1.7 times in real-world GPU applications involving multiple memory objects.

A recent initial principles theory helps explain the quantum states known as Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states that form when magnetic atoms, such as manganese, are placed on a superconducting surface like niobium. This theory takes into consideration the speed of light and quantum mechanical spin effects to better understand these states. When studying a single manganese atom and a pair of adjacent manganese atoms on the surface of niobium, calculations made using this theory closely match those from a standard theory, but also provide additional insights, such as explaining the orientation of the magnetic moments and explaining why a resonance occurs at a higher energy level for the pair of atoms.

The TOI-712 star system, which is located about 500 parsecs away from the Sun, was found to have multiple planets by Juan A. González, G. Valio, and their research team using data from the TESS mission. Initially, the light variations recorded by TESS were analyzed with a specific tool, which identified four candidates that were later confirmed as part of the system through high-resolution spectroscopy and radial velocity measurements. These planets, named TOI-712 b, c, d, and e, have orbital periods of 3.7, 7.1, 11.7, and 16.4 days respectively. TOI-712 d was found to be located just outside the star system's habitable zone, and it consists of an Earth-like core and an extensive hydrogen and helium atmosphere. A proposal is being made to observe a transit caused by TOI-712 d crossing in front of its star using the James Webb Space Telescope.
