This paper introduces an innovative concept called the "Elastic Potential" as a graphical tool to simplify interpretation of multivariate analysis in the context of particle physics research. We demonstrate its utility by developing a top-quark production analysis method for the Large Hadron Collider that relies solely on the final state hadrons to identify top-quark pairs. By utilizing simulated data, we established a top-quark pair production technique utilizing the Elastic Potential that yields better results than simpler approaches but falls short of leading-edge standards. However, this framework-based method can be easily integrated into more advanced anti-$\mathit{Q}_\mathrm{G}$ selections to enhance top-quark pair detection capabilities at the Large Hadron Collider.

Upper richness $\rho(G)$ of a graph $G$ was first defined by Erdős and Szemerédi in 1983, with initial applications in combinatorial geometry. We introduce the concept of upper richness for graph products and demonstrate that several infinite graph products have an infinite upper richness. Specifically, we prove the infinity of upper richness for the square of the cycle graph, the third power of the bipartite graph, and multiple other graph products including the Cartesian product $\square$, the lexicographic product $\cdot$, and the strong product $\otimes$.

Our quantum simulations of scalar QED in qudit systems lead to more efficient algorithms compared to qubit-based approaches. This improvement arises as the system memory requirements scale linearly with the spatial dimensions, and there's potential to increase the qudit dimension for a balanced trade-off between simulation capabilities and overhead.

Researchers investigated the positrons produced following the interaction of high-intensity laser pulses with dense targets, which had been exposed to lower-intensity lasers, and found that their polarization matched theoretical QED predictions for high-intensity single-beam interactions. This finding is notable, given the targets' thick nature and their complex composition consisting of multiple atom types. A significant level of positron polarization of approximately 20% was observed at approximately 20\% of the laser beam's critical power. Notably, a substantial level of intrinsic positron polarization was produced in this study despite the lack of intrinsic intrinsic particle polarization in the interactions of high-intensity lasers with targets. Furthermore, a region of enhanced positron polarization of up to 45% is predicted to exist at oblique interaction angles, which could prove valuable for several particle-physics and nuclear-physics experiments.

A group is said to be finite. Given a pair of elements in the group that stabilize under conjugation, denoted as $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the diameter of the group is defined as the maximum number of group elements $x$ for which $\alpha$ is equal to $\beta$ under multiplication by some power of $x$. A three-way relationship of equality between $\alpha$, $\beta$, and the square of $x$ is denoted as being in the diameter of the group. It is proven that the set of groups with a finite diameter is equivalent to the set of groups with a finite diameter squared.

To fill the gap in research and development, this project focuses on creating a compact sensor that can accurately monitor a device's temperature. The sensor developed for this purpose covers a 1.2-to-2.4V supply range and utilizes a dynamic biasing technique to track temperatures effectively. The final design covers a wide frequency range of 0 to 10MHz, and it was tested at various supply voltages and temperatures ranging from 0 to 100 degrees Celsius and 0.6 to 1.8 volts respectively. The results indicate that the sensor has an impressive temperature resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius, with a temperature detection range of 1.4 degrees Celsius and an overall system power consumption of 1.06 picojoules per degree Celsius. The developed sensor also has a compact area of 418,000 micrometers squared.

In this study, the fundamental concepts of submanifolds, normal bundles, and exact sequences are developed from a geometric perspective within the context of Lie groupoids and smooth stacks. Additionally, we establish the equivalence between geometric constructions on Lie groupoids and those on stacks, thereby demonstrating the validity of these concepts for use in the study of stacks. These equivalences enable the application of a recently introduced sequence defined on Lie groupoids to a specific instance of a Desensitizing map associated with smooth stacks.

Nonthermal amplitude growth in core clusters, a critical step in massive star formation, is supported by observations of the Dragon infrared dark cloud. The 850-micrometer continuum data from the Dragon core reveal 10 sources with line emissions at 1.1 mm, covering a 2.4 square degree area. A mass spectrum was derived from resolved sources, with mass values calculated using a far-infrared temperature of 17 K. At the 68% confidence level, a random distribution model failed to match the observed data, whereas a log-normal distribution fit the nonthermal density profile perfectly. This finding suggests that gravitational collapse and turbulence interactions are occurring within the core, essential components in creating massive stars.

Recurrence relations are highly valued in the study of random fields due to their ability to significantly reduce computational costs by relying solely on previously computed values. This enables efficient calculations, particularly for higher-order statistics and when working with skewed probability distributions. However, their utility is limited, as most multi-point correlations cannot be derived from two-point correlations through simple, closed-form relations in many widely used distributions. Our research reveals that for a specific class of distributions, static random fields on the sphere can be devised where all multi-point correlations are directly proportional to the square of two-point correlations. As practical applications of this breakthrough, we demonstrate that all multi-point correlations of a given distance can be calculated through just two iterations of single recurrences, specifically for Matern correlation functions at any $\nu$ value, and for Ricker wavelet at $\alpha=1$ at any scale.

The interplay of complex, ever-changing surface patterns known as dynamic self-sustained textures in liquid foams significantly influences friction. The study presents the first experimental evidence of this influence by measuring side forces between solid plates submerged in plate geometries, both at rest and in motion. The results show that plate interactions depend heavily on plate movement, geometry, and texture characteristics. A non-dimensional approach is proposed to explain the observed results by considering a new friction coefficient that accounts for texture effects. The proposed coefficient exhibits universal behavior across different plate movements and geometries. The findings suggest a new, unexpected role for self-sustaining dynamic textures in soft matter physics.

The prevalence of global skin cancer cases is escalating, necessitating the use of advanced detection methods. A key approach is the analysis of skin images, which can be enhanced through the use of deep learning techniques. Our proposed method employs a lightweight convolutional neural network (MCNN) with 13.5K parameters to identify four skin cancer types: melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, papillomacarcinoma, and actinic keratosis, achieving accuracies of 98%, 99%, 100%, and 99% respectively. Furthermore, we incorporate entropy calculations to detect anomalous samples, achieving 100% precision in identifying melanoma, BCC, and AK outliers, and 95% in identifying PCC outliers.

A horizontally placed, rapidly spinning heating pan is used in our experiment to demonstrate flexible fingers forming in a fluid- fluid Hele-Shaw setup. A polymer solution that is insoluble in water sits above water and creates flexible fingering patterns when injected through a small hole. The inertia of the spinning pan stabilizes an otherwise unstable interface between the two fluids. This device is capable of creating intricate, multi-arm patterns that change size and shape over time, and it has potential applications in microfluidics for creating intricate structures. A theoretical model is developed to capture the intricate patterns created in the experiment, and it shows that the pattern frequency is influenced by the angular velocity, the Rayleigh number, and the fluid properties, but not by the shape of the container.

A striking discovery of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (CC5H4CCH) has been made in the TMC-1 molecular cloud, indicating that complex organic molecules with both linear and cyclic carbon structures can coexist easily in interstellar space. Through the method of laboratory spectroscopy, researchers were also able to identify two other types of ethynyl cyclopentadiene in the same location. Notably, the abundance of these molecules is surprisingly on par with that of cyano cyclopentadiene, despite the generally lower stability of the ethynyl form. This finding contradicts the expectation that cyclic carbon structures with strong bonds would be more prevalent. For the TMC-1 model to match the observed abundances of all three molecules, a long-standing mystery regarding the high abundance of CCH and its derivatives has been addressed.

Neural machine translation(NMT) currently lacks the ability to handle future input effectively, a characteristic present in human translation. We propose a novel mechanism, future attention, to grant NMT systems this property. Our approach modifies the standard encoder-decoder architecture to enable the system to consider future target words when generating the current word. We experimentally evaluate our model over the standard NMT benchmark using the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation dataset. In addition to standard metrics, we assess performance based on difficult cases and difficult character errors. Our results show that future knowledge enhances system quality, reducing character error rate by 0.5%. Moreover, our results are better in difficult cases and difficult character errors.

The framework approach to software development gained popularity in the late 20th century. A key aspect of these frameworks was their ability to address specific computing applications. Researchers and practitioners began experimenting with framework-based approaches to developing software. In this paper, we investigate how frameworks were utilized in developing Grid software. We found that integrating framework principles into our existing software significantly enhanced its modularity, design, and design stability. This benefit was particularly apparent when new functionality needed to be added. However, we also encountered difficulties, primarily stemming from the lack of widely accepted standards at the time, which made translating the framework approach a challenging process. This paper explores how we addressed these difficulties, providing insights into applying framework approaches to complex software projects. Our findings are discussed in relation to prior research and have implications for the design of software frameworks.

A new version of combined dark fluid model that accounts for a specific level of dissipation is called the dissipative combined dark fluid model and is divided into two distinct fluid components: a non-relativistic cold dark fluid component and a ultra-relativistic radiation fluid component. A key feature of this model is the inclusion of a specific level of dissipation that it implies between these two components in a non-relativistic regime. The combined combined dark fluid model is reformed using a differential equation that can be compared to $\text{LCDM}$ model by applying the Tiago-Sa-Estebans method. The combined dark fluid model can be applied to a cluster of galaxies as an inference engine, employing the observable parameters such as X-ray gas mass, gravitational lensing mass, and total mass of the cluster. A dataset from the Abell 1689 cluster of galaxies is used for comparison and inference, with the required mass-to-light ratio and a best fit for the total mass profile of the cluster being determined. The results obtained from this model are found to be in line with established physical expectations and existing data.

Improper neutrino mass mechanisms and non-relativistic dark energy, potentially observable in future experiments, may arise from new interactions mediated by a scalar or axial-vector particle involving a neutrino-photon coupling and an additional invisible decay of a $J/\psi$ bosin. By analyzing these interactions in an effective field theory framework, we can establish constraints on five parameters defining the effective theory, leveraging both existing $J/\psi$ bosin decay data and future sensitivity of a XENONn-like experiment. These considerations imply that any such new physics would be undetectable in XENONn-like experiments.

This work introduces a novel multivariate functional singular cross-examination framework, building upon existing unilateral and multivariate methods, with a key distinction being its handling of both univariate and multivariate functional time series, either independently or combined. As such, this technique offers a flexible, integrated approach for analyzing multivariate functional data across various dimensional frameworks. The underlying CFSS-E algorithm leverages three examination tools to facilitate cross-examination, enabling transformation into the functional domain, singular value decomposition application in each domain, and cross-spectrum analysis in each domain, combined with morlet wavelet transformation as a reference. A Monte Carlo simulation study was conducted to evaluate the cross-examination framework's validity, followed by a real-world application to global temperature anomaly data. Furthermore, this study provides valuable insights into understanding interdependencies between different dimensional domains in multivariate functional data analysis.

A key property of a stochastic process is global persistence, which measures the joint probability that the process hasn't crossed a threshold within given time intervals for consecutive days. In contrast, local persistence focuses on the conditional probability of not crossing the threshold for one day, given it wasn't crossed the day before. While stochastic processes can be modeled using an autoregressive time series for local persistence, estimating global persistence requires more complex modeling due to its complex nature. A random walk in one dimension was modeled to estimate the relationship between global and local persistence, showing through simulation that global persistence accurately predicts the duration a random walk remains above its starting point for an extended period, with an average duration that matches the square of the persistence. These results can be utilized to develop more accurate models for predicting the prolonged behavior of processes exhibiting local persistence.

The small-scale helicon thruster technology relies on plasma generators that operate in the helicon mode, and to advance this technology, it is crucial to understand and control these plasma generators. The IShTAR experiment provides an ideal platform for this purpose, as it includes a plasma generator with the same design as the thruster, and offers advanced diagnostics to conduct detailed plasma analyses. This study aims to derive the plasma density and floating potential profiles, calculate the plasma flux to the walls, and the total plasma power, and to demonstrate the helicon mode operation by comparing the measured plasma parameters to those calculated from a 2D plasma generator code. The code successfully captures the main features of the measured parameters, and it is shown that the plasma power scales linearly with the magnetic field at low values, but becomes quadratic when the threshold is exceeded. The helicon threshold corresponds to the loss of plasma confinement when the larmor radius becomes too large, and this study also validates the plasma generator code, providing a baseline for future IShTAR discharge experiments and confirming the helical thruster's potential to achieve high specific impulses.

The microscopic examination of biological tissue is a widely used method for medical diagnosis.
However, this process relies heavily on the skills and knowledge of pathologists, who meticulously analyze individual cells within digital images of the tissue.
Automating this analysis through the use of deep learning has gained significant interest in recent years.
Despite the success of such models in classifying diseases at the image level or segmenting large features, they struggle with accurate nucleus segmentation.
Nucleus segmentation presents unique challenges, including low contrast, irregular shapes, and a vast range of sizes.
To address these difficulties, our research focuses on developing a novel end-to-end convolutional network called W-Net, inspired by successful cutting-edge models.
Our network employs an innovative two-stage design, which utilizes adjustable filter banks in its U-Net encoder to capture features at multiple frequencies.
Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of W-Net over other cutting-edge models, achieving improved nucleus segmentation accuracy in difficult breast cancer tissue images.
Specifically, our model outperforms the best comparable methods with a lower Dice Coefficient error of 0.1 on a challenging dataset, NUKS.

For any given nontrivial character $\chi$ of $k$, where $k$ is a finite field of an odd characteristic $p$, we establish the local converse theorem for the special orthogonal, orthogonal, and symplectic matrix groups of any fixed rank $n \geq 1$. Specifically, for any two generic test functions $f_\chi$ and $g_\chi$ on these matrix groups, the identities f_\chi(w) = g_\chi(u) hold if and only if u = w^{(-1)^{(p^n - 1)/2}}.

We aim to demystify the underlying mechanics of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), which have gained significant popularity in recent graph data processing applications. Our key contribution is the development of a novel interpretive framework for GCNNs, which equates their operations to a form of matching filtering. This hypothesis finds strong support through extensive theoretical analysis, empirical evidence, and practical examples. Building upon this foundation, we introduce a refined variant of the GCNN model that allows for a more meaningful interpretation of the learned convolutional features. This enhanced model achieves comparable accuracy to the state-of-the-art GCNN implementations in various graph-based classification tasks.

We expand a recent finding (arXiv:2009.00521) to include a scalar field, demonstrating that a specific Chern-Simons equation for the scalar field can precisely mimic the gravitational Chern-Simons action in a 3+1 dimensional spacetime. This analogy enables us to solve complex, nonlinear rotating black hole and boson star problems in general relativity. Notably, solutions to these problems feature an electric field that behaves like a Maxwell Chern-Simons effect in three dimensions. Moreover, we find a direct connection between these solutions and those of a purely 3+1 dimensional Einstein-Chern-Simons system, allowing us to generate black hole and boson star solutions to this latter system that avoid the issues of incorrect energy behavior at high angular momentum.

In ultrasound shear wave elastography, precise estimation of shear wave velocities is essential, particularly for recovering the waveforms at the waveforms' origins where spatial aliasing frequently distorts waveforms. A novel approach, called virtual origin synthetic aperture (VOSA), is introduced in this study to enhance the precision of waveforms origin estimation. By combining precise shear wave focuses using a synthetic aperture method in a synthetic virtual origin, VOSA overcomes the limitation of standard methods that result in spatially aliased waveforms. By comparing VOSA to the conventional synthetic aperture (ASA) method in simulations and a porcine liver, results show that VOSA provides more precise displacement aliasing periods and shear wave velocities, particularly in cases of spatial aliasing. Although the introduced algorithm increases the number of calculations, the utilization of inherently precise and sparsely populated axial displacements and the independence of VOSA from ASAs in time allow for acceptable processing times. Overall, VOSA is a promising approach for elastography applications that require precise shear wave velocities estimates in the waveforms' origin regions.

The concept of Rational Action Models has been introduced, building on the analysis of human behavior through Bayesian inference, in this work. By incorporating prior information about plausible actions, the category of Rational Action Models includes other models of human behavior, such as the Bayesian Rational Model and the Predictive Action Model as proven instances. A novel algorithm, called Rational Pseudocode, has been developed to capture demonstrated procedures from a teacher's actions. This algorithm uses a prior based on structural similarities to the target program, enabling more efficient learning from fewer demonstrations. In contrast, traditional methods like Replay and Trace require multiple repetitions of the procedure for accurate reconstruction. In experimental evaluations, Replay and Trace failed to train effectively using a single action model, whereas Rational Pseudocode achieved results comparable to these methods when multiple demonstrations were used.

The efficacy of unsupervised learning methods heavily relies on the accuracy of models they produce, which, in the case of a growing amount of input data, demands rapid and adaptable techniques. One such challenge is presented by dynamic learning methods that aim to incorporate multiple datasets comprising both instances and their associated groups based on a vast dimensionality. At its core, this problem involves combining multiple information sets that have been grouped according to their similarities, defined by a specific distance metric in a high-dimensional space. Existing solutions to this problem, primarily focused on a constant number of data sources, evaluate and combine tree-based representations of instances and groups using various distance metrics. However, these solutions are limited in their scalability due to their computational overhead in processing large datasets. This paper presents the first technique for dynamic groupings that processes every new instance and group with minimal memory access, achieving near-optimal performance compared to current methods while maintaining high adaptability in handling large amounts of information.

We've developed a novel framework to break down complex, unpredictable pursuit-evasion competitions significantly influenced by chance into distinct categories based on key turning points, dividing the matches into a hierarchy of three primary categories and a number of sub-categories with matching and evasion outcomes ranging from early-stage splits within the first quarter, mid-point divisions after the first half, to late-game splits in the final quarter, and also analyzing three specific, unpredictable competitions - a submarine hunt game, a polar bear capture competition, and a wolf pack hunting simulation - using this hierarchical breakdown framework.

A study is conducted to analyze the potential of a 1.5 TeV muon collider in discovering efficient production of W and Z bosons that result in specific decay patterns involving muons and neutrons, as well as muons and electrons. When considering precise assessments of this threshold with comprehensive considerations of higher-order corrections and existing crawler data, the most optimized detector achieves the ability to identify the relevant signals within a close proximity to the 1 TeV collision threshold with high accuracy. By considering various possible designs of the detector and comprehensive assessments of standard particle expectations, the study aims to establish the feasible limits of this challenging region of exploration.

In model-based reinforcement learning, combining multiple tasks models can improve single-task performance, but simultaneously learning those models can cause interference, leading to poor or inaccurate models and performance. Our research reveals that this cross-task information sharing can be as much as 200% in some scenarios, resulting in significant model inaccuracies and poor offline evaluation. To mitigate this issue, we propose a modular system that separates the learning of each tasks' models, our experiments show that this system reduces learning interference to near 10%, improving overall multi-task performance. Our findings are relevant to a wide range of real-world applications where multiple agents or models learn in shared environments, such as in urban traffic management.

This article is a discussion of the original works by four leading logicians whose individual cutouts fill the left page while their combined images fill the right when depicted according to their height, reach, arm length, and stride. Our examination delves into interconnections and contrasting ideas exchanged among them at the 1933 Berlin Individualistic Empiricism symposium in Copenhagen.

This research builds upon the "Three Spheres Theorem" in the context of functions, translating the concept of spheres to the evaluation of a specific function, $\Psi$, at non-spherical points. The study focuses on the relationship between the $L^2$ norms of this function at points located within an ellipsoid, given its norms at points on the ellipsoid and a surrounding shell can be determined. Reconstructing images from incomplete or noisy data is a challenging task with significant applications in various fields, such as medical imaging and remote sensing. This task is inherently ambiguous, as it involves inferring unobserved details and priorities that are not provided in the data. Traditional methods, including those based on deep learning, produce valid images that adhere to pixel-level accuracy, but they often fail to incorporate domain knowledge and result in diverse, unfavored solutions. To address this issue, we are in search of models that capture diverse solutions while also reflecting prior preferences. The challenge is further compounded by the computationally intensive nature of common approaches, which require multiple samples from a complex distribution. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a conditional generative adversarial network (DCCRGAN) that has two key features: it incorporates prior preferences in a computationally efficient manner and generates samples that align with both the available evidence and prior preferences with high diversity. We evaluate the proposed model on various imaging tasks, including magnetic resonance imaging from undersampled $k$-space data and X-ray tomography from limited-angle projections, and evaluate a simple variant of the model that uses a single point estimation. The results demonstrate the model's ability to produce images with high diversity, realistic features, and accurate reconstruction.

This article explores the concept of invariant manifolds within the context of dynamical systems that exhibit symmetry under transformation. We start by examining the definition of a invariant set and then proceed to prove that, in fractional-order systems with a degree n >= 2, no invariant manifolds exist. As a consequence of this proof, it becomes evident that the Heisenberg group cannot be represented as a manifold in a fractional-order system.

This research analyzes scintillation data from the bright pulsar PSR B1133+16 to map the local interstellar medium around us. By utilizing 12 days of data collected by the Parkes telescope at 408 MHz, we created 3D images of the local electron density turbulence at specific spatial frequencies. These models suggest that the turbulence spectrum follows a Kolmogorov pattern and that the distribution of spatial scales of irregularities is asymmetric, tilting at smaller scales. We also derived the characteristics of irregularities in space, including their asymmetry and tilt, and how they vary with distance. By comparing our findings with other research using very long baseline interferometry, we found that scintillometry provides a useful method for studying the local interstellar environment, although it is limited to specific areas and frequencies.

A Deep Neural Network called WaveNet generates audio waveforms directly through probabilistic modeling. By employing dilated convolution neural networks, Training efficiency and Training data requirements for WaveNet are significantly reduced. However, WaveNet's performance in generating speech is hindered by its reliance on training. This research proposes a modified architecture, called a Pitch-sensitive Dilated Convolution Neural Network (PD-CNN), to mimic the PD-CNN structure. The proposed model achieves a 25% reduction in perceived similarity distortion and a 15% reduction in mean opinion score when compared to the original WaveNet approach. The results indicate that the proposed Pitch-sensitive Dilated Convolution Neural Network (PD-CNN) model is able to generate more natural and high-fidelity speech.

The theory of shadows constitutes a strict 2-functor that establishes connections between the categories of bimodules and bimodule categories over a fixed algebra, and between the representations of two algebras. Given its rigid nature, it proves that the representations of an algebra are uniquely determined (up to Morita equivalence) by the algebra itself. When algebras are viewed as objects within a bicategory of bimodules, the shadow functions as a cohesive structure or, alternatively, as a bicategorical limit specific to bimodules. Furthermore, this document explores the concept of Morita stacks as equivalent structures to those with an algebra defined up to homotopy.

It frequently occurs that a student who outperforms their instructor takes on a teaching role with another, less skilled individual. This dynamic is mirrored in our work, where a former student, Dr. Aude Giraud, now an independent researcher at Uber, builds upon our published findings. The codebase is an extension of our previous work, originally developed in PyTorch3, and now encompasses additional functionalities in Java.

The success of graph neural networks in analyzing static graphs can be attributed in part to their ability to leverage labeled data through techniques like supervision and data augmentation. However, extending this advantage to dynamic graphs, and specifically time-evolving graphs that incorporate previous labels, is not straightforward. We investigate the feasibility of using historic labels from graphs with varying complexity over time, and find that such an approach, utilizing the surrounding context of a target node's past labels of the same class, enhances the performance of state-of-the-art methods for detecting potential faults. Our proposed method, the Lorentzian Graph Neural Network, adapts conventional neural network techniques to incorporate past labels, and successfully integrates both the spatial and temporal dimensions of graphs for various detection faults including corrupted edges, missing nodes, and altered attributes, as demonstrated in our experimental analysis.

This research examines a "reverse" mathematical problem associated with a structural acoustic interaction involving the Stefan condition, where we aim to determine an unknown boundary condition from given final domain information and final state data. The original problem initially involves a nonlinear partial differential equation within a specific domain, with associated local boundary conditions and an evolving domain through the Stefan condition on a moving boundary. The unknown condition is determined as a non-local boundary condition applied to a reference domain. Using optimal control techniques, we can establish the existence of a solution to this "reverse" problem. Additionally, we can prove the stable determination of this boundary condition when the known final domain and final data are given with high accuracy.

We developed a novel efficient delay discounting model, which we've named the Tsallis exponential model (TSED), to better fit a wide range of behavioral data. This approach stems from the application of non-extensive statistical mechanics, which led us to choose the Tsallis exponential function as the core of our model. Our model efficiently fits over 1100 datasets, primarily drawn from studies on rodent and human animal choice behavior involving short-term decisions, often referred to as microstructure delay discounting. These studies typically involve subjects making decisions between delayed rewards or cues for delayed rewards. We've also made two key predictions based on the TSED model and its underlying non-extensive non-additive nature, which we believe are testable through straightforward animal experiments. The TSED model makes subjects' preferences follow a transitive order, leading to two key predictions: 1) the order of delayed reward options adheres to a circular rather than linear order, and 2) the order of delayed cue conditions follows the opposite order when the actual rewards are swapped, even when the delay discounting curves for the two conditions are nearly identical.

We refer to a specific choice of gauge in substantial gravity as a harmonic gauge. Choosing a harmonic gauge in substantial gravity simplifies the field equations significantly. We demonstrate that two harmonic gauges lead to the same solution under certain conditions, which can be used to derive well-known gauge-based gravitic field theories.

This research examines the Wu-Tierney and Wu-Yang equilibrium conditions from a new perspective using Weyl and Wigner representations, revealing their connection to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. A general condition emerges that encompasses the Wu-Tierney condition as a special case. Furthermore, a novel interpretation of the Yang equation is obtained.

A minimally intricate extension of the Standard Model is proposed by adding a singlet field to both the scalar and gauge sectors, with specific self-couplings and interactions with a dark SU(2) gauge symmetry and the SM's HH potential. This model enables the calculation of the Higgs effective potential up to next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy. By exploring the parameter space, constraints from dark matter observations, electroweak precision measurements, and the measured signal strengths were analyzed. The model predicts a significant fraction of its dark matter to consist of charged particles that can be detected in the electromagnetic calorimeters of the LHC, with a distinct signature in the mass range of 25-45 GeV. The model also accounts for the leading order impact of two-loop corrections in the electroweak precision observables and in calculating the renormalization group evolution of the Higgs effective potential's renormalization scheme. In the range of 10 to 40 GeV for the dark matter mass, the model can naturally explain the muon anomalous magnetic moment discrepancy with previous findings. Additionally, the model's parameter space analysis was conducted considering the LHC and dark matter observations constraints, as well as the requirement for the vacuum stability of the HH potential up to the Planck scale. Results indicate that dark matter annihilation into the dark gauge bosons leads to an early universe reheat temperature below the Planck scale after inflation.

Blending of $t_{2g}$ orbitals with $e_g$ orbitals in transition metal compounds is typically hindered by symmetry, resulting in a seed for the Jahn-Teller effect that is relatively high.  This effect is usually seen in $d^1$, $d^4$, $d^6$, and $d^9$ electron configurations of transition metals in octahedral environments.  Nevertheless, we observe the Jahn-Teller effect in $d^3$ electron-deficient titanium compounds with an octahedral environment, a situation that is not usually associated with a significant degree of Jahn-Teller distortion.  Using a combination of experimental techniques and theoretical calculations, we uncover the root cause of this unusual behavior.  It turns out that the $t_{2g}$ blending is facilitated by removing symmetry constraints through the elimination of filled $t_{2g}$ orbitals and by the spatial size of 3d $t_{2g}$ orbitals.  As a consequence, we find that $d^3$ Ti compounds can exhibit a significant degree of Jahn-Teller distortion when the $t_{2g}$ symmetry is no longer protected, a situation that is not usually seen.

We developed a novel invariant, the relative quantum topology $\tau(M,f,\beta)$, which applies to a closed symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ with specific properties, including a symplectic form $\omega$ and certain divisors $f$. Nonetheless, our invariant undergoes unintended transformations when the underlying manifold undergoes certain topologically complex transformations known as blow-ups and inverse blow-ups. Nonetheless, this undesirable characteristic enabled us to intentionally perform such transformations on the blow-up of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ at one point, resulting in two distinct modified versions of the standard K3 surface, which we informally refer to as a "quantum topology" and its converse.

Overacting visualization techniques have attempted to depict medical findings by altering the structure of imaging data. Although these methods provide valuable supplementary information, their capacity to illustrate complex illnesses has been limited. This study introduces two sophisticated models - TCVA and TCCE, both based on conditional frameworks to depict a disease known as tuberculosis. TCCE, in particular, achieves the highest accuracy in recreating tuberculosis present in imaging data with a 92 F-score. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the practical application of synthesized images by illustrating their use in aiding diagnosis and determining the severity of a patient's illness. Notably, we found the modified visualizer hampers illness severity prediction when incorporating TCCE-generated images, yet it enhances this capability when using a TCVA model. Additionally, our study's attempt to reflect complex illnesses successfully allows for the customization of visual findings to reflect complex illnesses present in imaging data, in contrast to a single finding.

ViDaExpert is an interactive MATLAB utility for multidimensional vector visualization and analysis. It supports graphic displays of vector components, examination, sorting, and manipulation including graphing, scaling, rotation, examination, examination, and modification. With the ability to visualize vectors in 2D and 3D space using color, size, and shape, as well as a scrolable table for easy examination, sorting, and modification of vector elements, the tool is particularly effective for high-dimensional vectors that exceed human perceptual limits.
